subject.title: Bacchus III
subject.author: William Empson
subject.text:
The god who fled down with a standard yard
(Surveying with that reed which was his guard
He showed St. John the New Jerusalem;
It was a sugarcane containing rum
And hence the fire on which these works depend)
Taught and quivered strung upon the bend
An outmost crystal a recumbent flame
(He drinks all cups the tyrant could acclaim;
He still is dumb, illimitably wined,
Burns still his nose and liver for mankind) ...
It is an ether, such an agony.
In the thin choking air of Caucasus
He under operation lies forever
Smelling the chlorine in the chloroform.
The plains around him flood with the destroyers
Pasturing the stallions in the standing corn.

title: The Poem That Came With Its Own Answer Key
standfirst: William Empson put the hardest poem he ever wrote first in his 1940 collection, then attached six pages explaining it. Decoded, one stanza turns out to be built around a specific wartime atrocity story he had heard in China, and another around his own admission that the myth was flattering tyrants.

sections.heading: Fourteen Lines, No Key
sections.body:
In April 1940, [Poetry printed fourteen lines](https://archive.org/details/sim_poetry_1940-04_56_1) under the title "Bacchus III," credited to "William Empson" and set between a poem by Gladys Campbell and one titled "The Overturned Lake." There was no note, no gloss, nothing to tell a subscriber what to do with a god who flees "down with a standard yard," carries a reed that once measured out the New Jerusalem for St John and turns out on inspection to be "a sugarcane containing rum," and is then, without transition, found lying in "the thin choking air of Caucasus," smelling "the chlorine in the chloroform" while "the plains around him flood with the destroyers." A reader in 1940 had exactly what a reader has now: the poem, and nothing else.

That same year, Faber published the finished poem — ninety-two lines, of which this fragment is roughly a fifth — as the opening item in Empson's collection *The Gathering Storm*. This time it came armed. Six pages of [Empson's own prose](https://archive.org/stream/in.ernet.dli.2015.86596/2015.86596.Collected-Poems-Of-William-Empson_djvu.txt) followed it, explaining, phrase by phrase, what those fourteen lines are actually doing. He knew exactly how that would look before anyone complained: the book's preface to its own endnotes opens by admitting "these notes may well look absurdly pretentious, and they start off with the most extreme example." He put his hardest poem, and the longest key he ever wrote to unlock one, on page one.

He had a standing defence for this, repeated for years: a poem's difficulty is like a newspaper puzzle, and, as he told the [Criterion](https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v22/n12/frank-kermode/the-heart-of-standing-is-you-cannot-fly), "there would be no point in publishing a puzzle in a newspaper, if it were admittedly so simple that there was no need to publish the answer." "Bacchus" is the poem that tests how far he meant it.

sections.heading: The Reed Doing Three Jobs at Once
sections.body:
Empson's note divides the whole poem into four "verses," each built around a stage of a single conceit: the Bacchus myth, and the whole apparatus of Greek gods around it, restaged as a piece of laboratory equipment — "a mythological chemical operation to distil drink." What the magazine printed as "Bacchus III" is exactly what the note calls the third: "In the third verse the fire under the retort is given by Prometheus, who escaped from heaven with the gift of fire hidden in a reed."

That reed alone is carrying three unrelated stories. It is the stalk Prometheus supposedly hid stolen fire inside; it is, by way of the Book of Revelation, the measuring rod an angel uses to survey the New Jerusalem in Revelation 21, which is why the poem's god "showed St. John the New Jerusalem" with it; and because the fire under Empson's imaginary retort now comes from tyrants and invading cavalry as well as gods, the same reed becomes, in his own words, "a yard of the stallions, who appear now under Tartar horsemen." Three stories, one four-letter word, held together only by the fact that English lets "reed" carry all three without complaint. Empson built whole stanzas this way and called it punning, as if the method needed no further defence.

The torment gets the same treatment. "Taught is what he did, but he is now 'taut'," the note explains: "Prometheus stretched helpless along the glaciers is compared to the flame clinging to the glass of the retort, and its 'quivers' are supposed to eke out a hint at the arches of the Tartar bowmen." Even the vulture eating the chained god's liver is made to work twice, medically and psychologically at once: "one of the vultures at his liver may be cirrhosis and another remorse." And the poem's strangest single move — swapping Prometheus's mountain air for the smell of an operating theatre — turns out to be an admitted substitution rather than an accident: "Ether and chloroform smell to me much alike though only chloroform has got chlorine in it, so I swap drugs to bring in poison gas."

sections.heading: An Atrocity Filed Under Mythology
sections.body:
The gloss on the "Tartar horsemen" does not stop at wordplay. It continues: "the land round the Caucasus on which Prometheus is chained. In China it was felt as a major atrocity story that the Japanese had turned their horses into the ricefields, a thing apparently not done in the civil wars." That sentence does something the poem itself never announces: it tells the reader, in an offhand aside, that the excerpt's final image — "The plains around him flood with the destroyers / Pasturing the stallions in the standing corn" — is not classical set-dressing. It is a specific report Empson had heard described, by people living through it, as one of the things that marked this invasion off from China's own internal wars: an army grazing its cavalry in someone else's harvest.

He was in a position to hear it. [Empson had arrived in China in 1937](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Empson) for a post at Peking University that the Japanese invasion of the north had already erased that summer; he joined the ad hoc wartime faculty that reassembled first at Changsha and then, after Japanese bombing forced a further retreat, at Kunming, formalized in 1938 as [Lianda, the National Southwestern Associated University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Southwestern_Associated_University). "Bacchus" was among the poems he finished there before returning to England in January 1939 — a stretch of years the poem's own note treats less as tragic backdrop than as raw material: a rumor of atrocity, filed under a footnote to a myth about a wine god's suffering, offered with no more ceremony than the pun two sentences earlier.

One stanza before this, glossing an entirely different figure in the myth — Ixion, condemned in hell to a wheel of torture that Empson reads as also being the wheel of the turning earth — the note goes further still, in language too plain to be anything but deliberate: "I find the poem is giving hearty praise to people like Hitler and Mrs. Eddy in this aspect of Bacchus." A poem about the god of wine, decoded by its own author, turns out to be partly a poem about the appeal of demagogues.

sections.heading: A Poem Assembled Out of Order
sections.body:
"Bacchus" did not reach print as one object. Empson worked on it across roughly six years spanning his time in Japan and his years in wartime China, and [Poetry published pieces of it as he produced them](https://chinarhyming.com/2024/04/26/manchouli-william-empsons-china-poems-1/), not in the order the finished poem would eventually run. In January 1937, the magazine [printed a poem titled "Bacchus IV"](https://archive.org/details/sim_poetry_1937-01_49_4), under Empson's name, built on a small set of repeating end-words — despair, cope, arches, fire, cloud — in the manner of a sestina, describing a god who "snatched" a woman "into a cloud." Whatever this fourth movement was meant to become, it has almost nothing in common with the fourth verse Empson's later note actually describes: a section about Mercury, a burst thermometer, and a silver crucible eaten away by mercury. He scrapped it, or rewrote it past recognition, sometime in the three years before *The Gathering Storm* went to Faber.

Only after that, in April 1940, did Poetry print the section discussed above as "Bacchus III" — the piece above this feature. A subscriber who kept every relevant issue between 1937 and 1940 would have owned, out of sequence, an ending Empson later abandoned and a middle he had not yet finished annotating. The continuous ninety-two-line "Bacchus" that opens *The Gathering Storm*, keyed by its six-page note, did not exist anywhere as a single finished object until the book did.

sections.heading: Tricksy, and He Knew It
sections.body:
Empson was not blind to how the method looked from outside. Introducing [a recorded reading of "Bacchus"](https://www.thenation.com/article/archive/poet-duly-noted/), he warned his audience it would be "slightly tiresome to listen to, really, because it is so tricksy," and elsewhere admitted, in his own defence of his practice, to "an air of having to be clever all the time." He had built his notes deliberately against a model he half admired and half resented: T. S. Eliot's endnotes to *The Waste Land*, which Empson thought ["had to be written"](https://lib.uni-plovdiv.net/bitstream/handle/123456789/574/NTF_2012_50_1_D_206_216.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y) but which he also found guilty of a schoolmaster's tone and "an air of intellectual snobbery." His own notes, he insisted, should be chatty and good-humoured, never a lecture — and he thought withholding one, when a reader needed it, was the greater rudeness: "positively impertinent not to write [a note] which would save [the reader] further trouble."

The trouble it saves you, in this case, is not a classical education. It is the difference between reading fourteen lines about a god suffering on a mountain, in a vaguely operatic way any reader can nod along to, and reading fourteen lines in which a professor who had just heard how an invading army was treating the crops of the people sheltering him decided that image belonged inside a myth about the seductions of drink and power — and then, in his own hand, a few pages further into the same book, told you exactly where he had put it.
